and with swift feet he arrived in Egypt.
And he went and camped in a place called al-Mansurah, dense with trees,
and he raised a cry with zeal.
And bands of Arabs gathered to him from Alexandria, and from Qus and Aswan. But the people of the city of Damietta,
when they saw that the gaze of the Franks was directed toward them,
a panic fell upon them.
And without distress or battle they emptied the city of everything that was in it,
and they took their families and all their possessions and went to Egypt.
And the nobles of Damietta went to the Sultan,
and that al-Malik al-Salih asked them,
"Did the Franks press you hard in battle?" And they replied,
"No,
but we were afraid of that time, lest it draw us into the plight of Acre,
whom the Franks killed,
and no one helped them."
And al-Salih was enraged against them, and he hanged 64 {or 60? in text: 64: 'and 64 nobles'} famous nobles upon thirty-two crosses,
in pairs,
just as they were in their garments and even in their sandals (and in their shoes).
And when they had crucified these,
he too, after a few days, died from an evil ulcer that broke out on his thigh,
and it was completely severed from him as it was,
and fell off.
And the Egyptian nobles sent and fetched al-Malik al-Mu'azzam, the son of al-Salih,
who was at that time in Hisn Kayfa,
and they made him king in place of his father.
And his regent was Fakhr al-Din Uthman, son of the Shaykh al-Shuyukh, the grand vizier.
The Franks, however, approached the wall of Damietta,
and did not hear the sound of a watchman at all,
nor did any human being appear to them on the battlements,
and they were astonished.
And they sent men again, and they entered inward from the harbor,
and they did not encounter a human being.
And they knew that they had fled away in flight.
And they drew near and entered the city in great quietness and joy.
And that day was a Friday.
And they did not find in it anyone that pisseth against the wall.
And ships were supplying them with all provisions from the sea.
However, their reckless mind did not allow them to wait patiently until they learned the custom of the country and the crossings of the rivers and the roads,
but they hastened and crossed a tributary of the Nile, and marched away from the water toward Egypt along a waterless road.
